opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The core point of trying to define superintelligence carefully is to replace vibes with something you can measure. For years "AGI" and "superintelligence" have been moving goalposts: every time a system does something impressive, people say "well, that's not *real* intelligence." If you instead define these things in terms of concrete capabilities, essentially how broad the range of cognitive tasks is where a system matches or beats humans, and how far it exceeds us on them, you can actually track where we are on the curve.

When I look at current progress through that lens, what strikes me is how much of the path we've already covered. On a growing list of tasks, including coding, mathematics, scientific reasoning, persuasion, and much of the knowledge work people do at their desks, these systems are at or above the level of most humans, and they keep improving. The remaining gaps, like long-horizon autonomy, reliability, and some forms of physical-world competence, are real. But they're shrinking quickly, and many of the people building these systems say openly that they expect to close them within a few years.

For safety standards, the implication is simple: you don't wait until you've crossed the line to start writing the rules. We'd never let a pharmaceutical company say, "Let's release the drug first and set up the FDA once we see whether people get hurt." Every other powerful technology, from medicines and airplanes to nuclear reactors, has binding safety standards that you have to meet *before* deployment, and the burden of proof is on the company, not the public. AI is the odd one out. Right now there's less regulation on building something that could be smarter than all of us than on opening a sandwich shop.

A clear definition helps here because it lets you set thresholds in advance. You can say: once a system demonstrates these capabilities, it must meet these safety requirements, such as showing it can't help make bioweapons, can't escape human control, and won't deceive its operators, before it's deployed or even trained further. That's far better than arguing after the fact about whether something "counts."

So my reading of the timing is that we're late, not early. The capability curve has outpaced the policy curve. The good news is that this is a solvable problem. We know how to do safety standards; we've done it for every other industry. What we need is the political will to treat AI companies like every other company, and to insist that controllable, beneficial tools come before uncontrollable superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes remaining capability gaps and says systems have covered much of the path, but it does not clearly state that current systems have not yet reached AGI under the paper’s definition.

r002.rationale: The response says safety standards are already late and capabilities may close remaining gaps within a few years, but it does not warn that standards introduced in three to five years could arrive only after AGI has been created.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The reason I wanted a careful definition in the first place is that the word "superintelligence" had become almost useless. People were using it to mean everything from "better than me at chess" to "a god in a box," and you can't write a safety standard around a word that slippery.

So the approach in the paper is to stop treating intelligence as a single number and instead ask a very concrete question: on a given task, does the system outperform the best humans who do that task? And then, how broad is the set of tasks where that's true? That gives you a spectrum. At one end you have narrow superintelligence, which we've obviously had for a long time, since no human beats a computer at multiplying large numbers. At the other end you have something that beats essentially all humans at essentially all cognitively relevant tasks, including the tasks that matter for power, like strategy, persuasion, engineering, and designing better AI.

When I look at current systems through that lens, I think the honest reading is that we're already in the uncomfortable middle. These models are superhuman along a growing number of dimensions, things like breadth of knowledge, speed, reading and writing code, passing professional exams. And they're still clearly subhuman along others, like long-horizon planning, reliability, and acting coherently in the physical world. The important observation isn't where the frontier is today. It's how fast the superhuman region is expanding, and that it's expanding into exactly the capabilities that are relevant for losing control.

And that's really the point about timing. If you define superintelligence as the endpoint, the thing that's better than us at everything, then you'll conclude we should wait to regulate until we see it. But that's backwards, because by that definition the moment you can confirm it exists is the moment it's too late to impose standards from a position of strength. Every other powerful technology, from aviation to pharmaceuticals to nuclear power, we required safety demonstrations before deployment, not after the first catastrophe. I don't see why AI should be the one exception.

So my answer is that current progress tells me the time for binding safety standards is now, not when some threshold is crossed. The definition is useful precisely because it lets you make the standards graded. You can say: if a system is superhuman in these specific domains, autonomous cyber operations, bioengineering, self-improvement, then here's the quantitative safety case the company has to make before release, the same way we don't let a drug on the market because the CEO says it feels safe. The companies themselves say they're a few years from the full version. If you take them at their word, you don't start writing the rules a few years from now. You start writing them today.

r001.rationale: The response says current systems are superhuman in some areas and subhuman in others, but it does not state that they have not reached AGI under the paper’s definition.

r002.rationale: It urges starting standards now and mentions companies being a few years from the “full version,” but does not warn that standards introduced in three to five years could come only after AGI has been created.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish two questions: How capable are these systems becoming, and how much assurance do we need before deploying them? A definition of superintelligence helps clarify the first question, but we shouldn’t make crossing that threshold the trigger for taking safety seriously.

Current progress is uneven. AI can be extraordinarily capable at some tasks and still fail at things humans find straightforward. So I wouldn’t infer from a striking demonstration that we’ve reached general superintelligence. But those limitations aren’t a guarantee of safety, either. A system doesn’t have to outperform us at everything to cause substantial harm.

For timing, the key point is that developing standards, evaluations, and oversight takes time. If we wait until everyone agrees that a system is superintelligent, we’ve waited too long. We should establish safety requirements now, strengthen them as capabilities and autonomy increase, and require evidence that the risks are adequately controlled before consequential deployment. Uncertainty about the arrival date is a reason to prepare, not a reason to postpone preparation.

r001.rationale: The response says a striking demonstration alone would not justify inferring that general superintelligence has been reached, but it does not clearly state that current systems have not reached AGI under the paper’s definition.

r002.rationale: It warns that waiting for agreement on superintelligence could be too late, but does not mention FDA-style standards or the three-to-five-year timeframe, nor say standards might arrive after AGI is created.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish impressive performance on particular tasks from the breadth of capability that would make a system superintelligent. A system can be much better than us at some things and still be surprisingly bad at others. So you shouldn’t take a spectacular benchmark result as proof that we’ve crossed that threshold. But you also shouldn’t take the remaining weaknesses as reassurance that we have plenty of time.

For safety standards, the relevant question is: how much warning will we have, and how long does it take to put meaningful safeguards in place? There’s enormous uncertainty about the first, while we know that developing standards, testing systems, and building institutions takes time. That argues for doing the work now.

I’d like the burden to be on developers to demonstrate that sufficiently powerful systems meet appropriate safety requirements before deploying them. We don’t need to settle the exact date of superintelligence to agree on that. A definition helps clarify the destination; it shouldn’t become an excuse to postpone precautions until we’ve arrived.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes task performance from broad superintelligence, but does not state that current AI systems have not reached AGI under the paper’s definition.

r002.rationale: It argues for starting safety work now, but does not mention FDA-style standards, a three-to-five-year delay, or the risk that standards would arrive after AGI is created.
